summary:
Sexual conduct between people of the same sex has been legal since the Penal Code took effect in November 2012, and the provision covers both male and female activity. The age of consent applies equally regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity, but the sources disagree on the figure: two record it as 16, while others report that Law 15/2021, the First Amendment to the Penal Code, raised it to 18 in 2021. A visitor should assume 18 until the discrepancy is resolved, because if the higher figure is correct it applies to visitors as well as residents.

São Tomé and Príncipe has no legal gender-identity recognition. No procedure exists for changing the sex or gender marker on an identity document, so a traveller whose passport, visa or other papers do not match their presentation carries that mismatch into every inspection with no domestic remedy behind it. Border, immigration and hotel staff see the discrepancy wherever documents are checked, and national law and policy say nothing about how such a case should be handled.

No form of relationship recognition exists. Same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are not recognised and adoption by such couples is not available. A trans visitor whose relationship is locally classed as same-sex, or read as same-sex from recorded birth sex, has no route to have a partner recognised for next-of-kin, medical decision-making, immigration or inheritance purposes.

Article 16.2 of the 2019 Labour Code prohibits workplace discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. There is no general anti-discrimination protection beyond employment, so the ban does not reach housing, healthcare, goods and services, or public accommodation. Neither the Labour Code nor any other cited provision names gender identity, which means the employment protection does not on its face cover a trans employee dismissed or harassed for being trans.

Article 130(2)(d) of the Penal Code makes crimes motivated by hatred of the victim's sexual orientation eligible for enhanced sentencing. As with the employment provision, the listed ground is sexual orientation and gender identity is not included. No hate-crime provision naming gender identity and no trans-specific protection machinery are documented.

The available sources record no trans-specific violence, enforcement action or protection outcome, and none of them makes a separate finding on societal tolerance of trans people as distinct from LGBTQ people generally. LGBTQ people are described as facing stigmatisation among the wider population. Taken together, the law here does not criminalise a trans visitor, but it offers no recognition, no document remedy and no protection ground that names them.
tangentialFactors:
São Tomé and Príncipe signed the United Nations joint statement on ending acts of violence and related human rights violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity. The signature condemns violence and discrimination at the international level; it creates no domestic enforcement mechanism, no complaints body and no protection that a visitor or resident can invoke in practice.

Both statutory protections that exist turn on sexual orientation rather than gender identity, so a trans visitor seeking to rely on them would have to fit their situation into a sexual-orientation ground. The inventory contains no comparative or regional material on trans visitors, and no consular or bilateral arrangement bearing on document mismatch.
localsOnly:
A 2016 poll found that 46% of São Toméans would like or not mind having an LGBTQ neighbour. The question does not separate attitudes toward trans people from attitudes toward LGBTQ people generally, and no trans-specific survey result is available.

The employment discrimination ban in Article 16.2 of the 2019 Labour Code is the only anti-discrimination provision in force and matters mainly to people working in the country. It gives a resident employee a stated ground in a dismissal or harassment claim brought on sexual-orientation grounds, does not name gender identity, and does not extend to services, housing or healthcare.

LGBTQ residents are described as facing stigmatisation among the broader population. That description is general and is not broken down by trans status, so it says nothing precise about how a trans resident or visitor is received outside the law.
outOfScopeNotes:
The age of consent is unresolved. Two sources state 16, equal for everyone. Two others state that Law 15/2021 raised it to 18 in 2021. No primary text of the amendment appears in the inventory.

No source records an enforcement action, court ruling, police practice or government statement bearing on trans travellers in São Tomé and Príncipe. The absence of documented trans-specific incidents is an absence of monitoring and reporting, not evidence that none occur.

All four cited sources are encyclopaedic and restate the same small set of provisions, so the account of the law is consistent but thinly sourced. Nothing in the inventory reports how the Labour Code ban or the Penal Code sentencing provision has been applied in practice.

Whether the omission of gender identity from those two provisions has ever been litigated or administratively interpreted is not sourced.
